study_material.title: Financial Statement Analysis & Ratios
study_material.introduction: Once you can read the three statements, the next skill is analyzing them: profitability margins, working capital efficiency, and the liquidity/leverage ratios that tell you whether a company can pay its bills and service its debt. This is standard ground in any finance interview, from FP&A to credit analysis to equity research.
learning_objectives: Calculate and interpret gross, operating, net, and EBITDA margins
Explain working capital and the cash conversion cycle
Compute DSO, DIH, and DPO and know what each measures
Distinguish ROA, ROE, and ROIC and explain how leverage links ROA to ROE
Identify the key liquidity, leverage, and coverage ratios used in credit analysis

concepts.heading: 1. Profitability Margins
concepts.body: Gross Margin = Gross Profit / Revenue (efficiency of production). Operating Margin = EBIT / Revenue (core profitability, independent of capital structure and taxes). Net Margin = Net Income / Revenue (bottom-line profitability, affected by financing and taxes). EBITDA Margin = EBITDA / Revenue - the most widely used margin for cross-company comparison since it strips out both capital structure (interest) and non-cash items (D&A).

concepts.heading: 2. Working Capital & the Cash Conversion Cycle
concepts.body: Working Capital = Current Assets - Current Liabilities, a measure of near-term liquidity. Net Working Capital (NWC) excludes cash and debt since they're non-operating. Three efficiency ratios matter: Days Inventory Held (DIH = Inventory/COGS x 365 - time to sell inventory), Days Sales Outstanding (DSO = AR/Revenue x 365 - time to collect from customers), Days Payable Outstanding (DPO = AP/COGS x 365 - time taken to pay suppliers). Cash Conversion Cycle = DIH + DSO - DPO: the number of days cash is tied up before it's converted back to cash. Lower is better.

concepts.heading: 3. Return Ratios: ROA, ROE, ROIC
concepts.body: Return on Assets (ROA) = Net Income / Average Total Assets - how efficiently assets generate profit. Return on Equity (ROE) = Net Income / Average Shareholders' Equity - how efficiently shareholder capital is used. Without debt, ROA and ROE are equal; adding leverage raises ROE above ROA (since equity, the denominator, shrinks relative to assets). Return on Invested Capital (ROIC) = NOPAT / Invested Capital - compared against WACC, a company earning ROIC above its cost of capital is creating value.

concepts.heading: 4. Credit Analysis Ratios
concepts.body: Liquidity ratios (Current Ratio = Current Assets/Current Liabilities, Quick Ratio - stricter, only highly liquid assets) show whether short-term obligations can be met. Leverage ratios (Debt/EBITDA, Debt/Equity) show how much debt is used relative to earnings or capital. Coverage ratios (EBITDA/Interest Expense, Debt Service Coverage Ratio) show whether cash flow can service debt payments - a DSCR below 1.0x is a red flag.

formulas: Gross/Operating/Net/EBITDA Margin = (Gross Profit / EBIT / Net Income / EBITDA) / Revenue
DIH = (Inventory / COGS) x 365; DSO = (AR / Revenue) x 365; DPO = (AP / COGS) x 365
Cash Conversion Cycle = DIH + DSO - DPO
ROA = Net Income / Average Total Assets; ROE = Net Income / Average Shareholders' Equity
Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities
shortcut_methods: EBITDA margin is the default 'apples-to-apples' profitability comparison across companies with different debt levels and tax situations - reach for it first when comparing peers
Lower DSO/DIH and higher DPO are all 'good' for cash conversion cycle - the company collects fast, sells inventory fast, and pays suppliers slowly
ROE > ROA is not automatically bad - it just means the company uses leverage. Check whether the leverage is sustainable (via coverage ratios) before judging it as risky
common_mistakes: Comparing net margins across companies with very different capital structures or tax jurisdictions - use EBITDA or operating margin for a cleaner comparison
Treating negative working capital as automatically bad - some efficient businesses (fast inventory turnover, slow supplier payment) run on negative working capital by design
Forgetting that ROA and ROE use AVERAGE (not ending) assets/equity, since the income statement numerator covers a period while the balance sheet denominator is a snapshot
study_material.summary: Ratio analysis translates raw financial statements into comparable, standardized signals: margins for profitability, DSO/DIH/DPO and the cash conversion cycle for working-capital efficiency, and ROA/ROE/ROIC plus liquidity/leverage/coverage ratios for overall financial health and creditworthiness.
quick_revision_notes: EBITDA margin = most comparable profitability metric across peers (capital-structure and tax neutral)
Cash Conversion Cycle = DIH + DSO - DPO; lower is better
ROE = ROA when no debt; leverage pushes ROE above ROA
ROIC > WACC means the company is creating value with its capital allocation
DSCR < 1.0x signals the company may not generate enough cash to service its debt

practice_questions.question: Which margin is most commonly used to compare profitability across companies with different capital structures and tax rates?
practice_questions.explanation: EBITDA margin excludes interest (capital structure), taxes, and non-cash D&A, making it the most standardized basis for cross-company comparison.

practice_questions.question: A company has DIH of 40 days, DSO of 30 days, and DPO of 25 days. What is its cash conversion cycle?
practice_questions.explanation: Cash Conversion Cycle = DIH + DSO - DPO = 40 + 30 - 25 = 45 days.

practice_questions.question: A company has ROA of 10% and a 50/50 debt-to-equity capital structure. What is its approximate ROE?
practice_questions.explanation: With $100 in assets, 10% ROA implies $10 net income. With equity at only $50 (50/50 D/E), ROE = $10/$50 = 20% - leverage amplifies ROE above ROA.

practice_questions.question: A Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR) below 1.0x most likely indicates:
options: The company may not generate enough cash flow to cover its debt obligations
The company has no debt at all
The company's inventory turns over quickly
practice_questions.correct_answer: The company may not generate enough cash flow to cover its debt obligations
practice_questions.explanation: DSCR compares available cash flow to required debt payments; below 1.0x means cash flow is insufficient to cover those obligations, a warning sign for creditors.

practice_questions.question: Company A has an ROIC of 15% and a WACC of 9%. Company B has an ROIC of 8% and a WACC of 9%. What can you conclude?
options: Company A is creating value from its capital allocation; Company B is destroying value
Both companies are creating equal value
Company B is performing better because its WACC and ROIC are closer
ROIC and WACC cannot be compared this way
practice_questions.correct_answer: Company A is creating value from its capital allocation; Company B is destroying value
practice_questions.explanation: A company creates value when ROIC exceeds its cost of capital (WACC). Company A's 15% ROIC > 9% WACC creates value; Company B's 8% ROIC < 9% WACC destroys value.
